rationale: The evidence pack shows Deel's API, MCP server, and payroll/global hiring capabilities, but there is no mention of any QuickBooks/Xero integration or automated syncing of payroll journal entries to accounting software.

Deel exposes a REST API and MCP server that can create contractor contracts, list contracts, and expose payroll/people data to agents, showing some building blocks for agent-driven onboarding. However, the evidence pack shows no explicit endpoint or MCP tool for full employee creation with compensation and tax setup (only contractor contract creation and cost-comparison tools are documented).

Deel documents API/MCP tools for contracts, time-off, and EOR cost comparisons, but no evidence of an endpoint or MCP tool that runs a payroll preview or surfaces anomalies for review before approval.

Deel exposes payroll, contracts, and people data via REST API and an MCP server that lets AI agents pull this data (deel-docs-2, deel-docs-8, deel-docs-15, deel-docs-23), which supports the 'pull via API' half of the story. However, there is no evidence of a payroll journal/GL export format or reconciliation-into-ledger functionality—no mention of accounting journal entries, chart-of-accounts mapping, or ledger sync tools.

Probes confirm a working llms.txt (HTTP 200) and markdown-accessible docs (.md suffix), plus a documented MCP server with tool references, directly enabling agent-oriented consumption of Deel's docs and APIs.

Deel doesn't show native in-app AI insights/suggestions, but it does expose contracts, payroll, people, and time data via an MCP server to external AI agents (Claude, ChatGPT) that can then generate insights or run calculations like EOR-vs-entity cost comparisons.

Deel offers webhooks for event-driven integration and an MCP server exposing tools (e.g., createTimeOffRequest, listOfContracts) that AI agents can invoke, enabling agent-triggered actions, but these are agent-invoked or event-triggered actions rather than evidence of true autonomous, self-scheduling background automation workflows. No evidence of built-in autonomous scheduling/orchestration for unattended background runs beyond webhooks + API/MCP tool calls.

Deel does not appear to have a native, built-in AI assistant embedded in its own product UI; instead it exposes an MCP server that lets external AI agents (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor) invoke Deel operations like creating time-off requests or listing contracts, effectively enabling delegation but only through third-party AI clients.

Deel offers a well-documented REST API, sandbox environment, webhooks, and even an MCP server enabling programmatic/headless automation of contracts, payroll, and time-off requests—strong support for CI/agentic workflows. However, there's no explicit evidence of CLI tooling, API keys/service-account auth for CI pipelines, or community validation of headless reliability, and some negative community feedback raises concerns about rigid workflows and support quality.

All evidence shows Deel exposes its own MCP server so external AI assistants (Claude, ChatGPT) can call Deel's tools — the reverse of the story, which asks whether a user can plug external MCP servers into Deel so Deel can use their tools. No evidence indicates Deel acts as an MCP client consuming other servers' tools.

Deel provides an official documented MCP server exposing platform tools (contracts, time-off, EOR calculations) with OAuth2 support for clients like Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, and VS Code, confirmed via docs and probe.

Deel provides an official MCP server exposing platform actions (create time-off, list contracts, compare EOR costs) so AI agents like Claude/ChatGPT/Cursor can operate it via natural language, with OAuth2 handled automatically by most clients. However, this is all vendor documentation with no independent/community validation of real-world natural-language usage, and other community feedback highlights rigid workflows and poor handling of exceptions, raising doubt about how flexible true natural-language control is in practice.
Evidence shows Deel offers a REST API and an official MCP server for AI agents, but there is no mention anywhere in the docs or probes of an official command-line interface (CLI) tool.

Deel provides a well-documented public REST API with endpoints (contracts, payroll, people), a sandbox for testing, webhooks, and even an official MCP server exposing structured tools for AI agents like Claude/ChatGPT—directly matching the ai-native/agenticness axis. Probes confirm docs are live and machine-readable (llms.txt, .md endpoints).

The evidence shows Deel has an MCP server and OAuth2 authorization flow for agent access, but there is no mention of scoped or least-privilege API credential/token issuance (e.g., granular permission scopes, role-limited API keys) for agents.

Deel offers documented REST APIs, a sandbox, webhooks, and an official MCP server exposing tools like createTimeOffRequest and listOfContracts for AI agent integration, satisfying the agentic/AI-native use case. However, there's no evidence of official language SDKs (e.g., Python, Node client libraries) beyond raw REST endpoints and MCP tool schemas, and community feedback raises reliability/trust concerns about the platform generally.

Deel's developer docs explicitly document a webhooks system delivering real-time event notifications with HMAC-SHA256 signature security, avoiding polling — directly matching the subscribe-to-events story.

Deel provides API docs, an API sandbox with pre-populated test data, and an MCP server exposing callable tools with structured JSON I/O, which supports agentic exploration and testing. However, there is no explicit evidence of an interactive API reference UI with in-browser runnable code examples (e.g., a Swagger/OpenAPI try-it console).

Deel has extensive REST API docs, a sandbox, MCP tools reference, and llms.txt/markdown-friendly docs (probes confirm machine-readable doc pages), but no direct evidence of a downloadable OpenAPI/Swagger spec file being offered.

Deel's official docs describe a dedicated API Sandbox that is a separate environment pre-populated with sample contracts, workers, and organizations, allowing safe API testing without touching production data, and supports resetting to restore original test data.

The evidence shows an API sandbox and a 'stable' API path, implying some versioning, but there is no mention anywhere of a documented deprecation policy, version lifecycle, or breaking-change guarantees for Deel's API.

Deel markets 'automated compliance' and global/US payroll processing across countries, implying tax handling, but no evidence explicitly confirms automated federal/state/local tax calculation, filing, and remittance specifics or IRS/state agency integrations; community complaints also raise concerns about rigid, buggy workflows undermining reliability.

Deel's documented API and MCP tools (createTimeOffRequest, listOfContracts, contract creation) are single-item operations; there is no evidence of bulk/batch endpoints or MCP tools supporting multi-item operations in one call.

Deel provides webhooks for real-time event notifications (e.g., HMAC-signed) and an MCP server exposing tools/actions (createTimeOffRequest, listOfContracts, etc.) that AI agents can invoke, giving the building blocks for event-driven automation. However, there's no evidence of a native rules engine where users define 'if event X then action Y' logic within Deel itself—automation requires external glue code or agent orchestration.

Evidence shows Deel's API, webhooks, and MCP server enable event-driven integrations and on-demand tool calls (e.g., listOfContracts, createTimeOffRequest), but there is no documentation of a scheduler, cron-like trigger, or recurring workflow/automation feature for AI agents to set up recurring jobs.

No evidence in the pack shows any automation versioning, review, or rollback capability for Deel's API, MCP server, or webhooks; documentation covers API/MCP tool references and sandbox testing but nothing about versioning or rolling back automations/workflows.

No evidence in the pack describes any capability to cancel, void, or correct a submitted payroll run before pay-out; docs cover contracts, sandbox, webhooks, and MCP tools but nothing about payroll run correction/cancellation, and community feedback highlights rigid, unhelpful workflows.

Evidence shows Deel offers payroll/compliance execution, APIs, webhooks, and MCP tools, but nothing describes proactive alerting for new-hire, location, or law-change compliance obligations. Community evidence focuses on unrelated data/wallet complaints.

Evidence shows a general Deel REST API, webhooks, and MCP integrations for AI agents, but nothing about a white-label or embeddable partner API that lets developers rebrand and embed Deel's payroll UI/flows into their own product.

Deel's marketing claims broad 'run accurate, compliant payroll' across 150+ countries, implying standard payment methods, but no evidence specifies next-day/2-day direct deposit timing. Community reports describe Deel forcing payees onto a 'Deel Wallet' stored-balance card with restrictive terms rather than straightforward bank direct deposit, directly undercutting the story's premise.

The evidence pack shows Deel's general payroll and API/MCP capabilities but contains no mention of configuring multiple pay schedules (weekly, biweekly, semimonthly, monthly) per team, so there's no direct proof of this specific ops capability.

Deel's marketing and docs clearly claim EOR and global payroll across 150+ countries with tools to compare EOR vs entity hiring, contract creation APIs, and payroll consolidation—supporting the founder's ability to employ internationally. However, community reports describe serious operational issues (data misuse, forced Wallet payment terms, rigid workflows, poor support) that add significant real-world caveats to the otherwise well-documented capability.

Evidence covers payroll, contracts, EOR, MCP/API tooling, but nothing about offering or administering health insurance, benefits enrollment, or deduction syncing to payroll — this specific benefits-admin capability is unaddressed in the pack.

Deel's docs and marketing clearly claim global contractor payments and compliant contracts across 150+ countries with API/contract creation support, but community reports describe payment platform issues (forced Deel Wallet with punitive arbitration terms), rigid/buggy workflows, and poor customer service handling exceptions, undermining the smooth compliant-payment experience.

Deel markets broad 'compliant payroll' across 150+ countries and consolidating multiple vendors, implying tax/withholding handling, but no evidence specifically addresses US multi-state registrations or withholding logic. Community feedback also raises reliability and rigidity concerns that could affect compliance execution.

Evidence shows Deel runs global payroll and has APIs for contracts, time-off, and general payroll processing, but there is no mention anywhere of off-cycle payroll runs, bonus/correction payments, or termination-triggered pay-outs outside the regular schedule.
Evidence covers contracts API, payroll, MCP server, and sandbox, but no mention of offer letter generation, e-signature workflows, or per-employee document storage/repository features.

Deel offers a broad REST API (contracts, payroll data) plus an MCP server exposing many operations (time-off requests, contract listing, EOR cost calculations) and webhooks/sandbox tooling, indicating substantial API coverage of core workflows. However, there is no explicit claim or evidence of full UI-API parity, and community feedback describes rigid workflows and persistent UI bugs, suggesting some functionality may not be fully exposed or automatable via API.

Deel's REST API and MCP tools (e.g., listOfContracts) let a technical user programmatically pull contract/payroll/people data as JSON, which could support an export/leave workflow, but there is no documented bulk-export feature, no stated open-format data portability guarantee, and community feedback raises concerns about Deel's data practices rather than confirming easy exit/export.

Deel is a closed-source commercial SaaS platform; no evidence in the pack indicates any open-licensed source code availability. Evidence only covers API docs, MCP server, sandbox, and community complaints, none relating to source code openness.
Deel is a SaaS global payroll/HR platform with no self-hostable core product; self-hosting doesn't apply to this type of cloud service.

Deel's own docs and marketing clearly claim unified payroll for employees, contractors, and EOR workers across 150+ countries with a documented API/MCP for contracts and payroll, supporting the story on paper. However, community evidence describes operational friction, rigid workflows, and issues with payment mechanisms (forced Deel Wallet, offboarding bugs) that suggest real-world execution of paying diverse worker types is not as seamless as claimed.

Deel documents a webhooks system delivering real-time notifications for platform events secured with HMAC signatures, supporting the general capability, but the evidence pack does not list specific payroll lifecycle event types (e.g., payroll processed, employee onboarded, payment failed) or subscription mechanics, so full coverage of the named events can't be confirmed.

Evidence shows Deel runs global payroll and exposes contracts/payroll data via API/MCP, but there is no mention of payroll register or gross-to-net report generation/export functionality anywhere in the pack.

No evidence in the pack mentions data residency, regional storage options, or GDPR/region-specific hosting controls for Deel; instead there are community complaints about data misuse, suggesting no visible residency controls.

No evidence pack items mention an AI-training data opt-out, privacy controls over model training, or any related policy; instead, community evidence raises concerns about Deel's data-handling practices (e.g., using contact data for marketing without consent) and lack of privacy controls.

No evidence pack items address data retention or deletion controls; the only privacy-adjacent evidence is community complaints about unauthorized data use, not about retention/deletion controls themselves.

No evidence pack items mention telemetry, usage tracking, or an opt-out mechanism for AI/agent usage; community evidence even suggests Deel aggressively collects and uses data without consent, but nothing addresses a telemetry opt-out control.

Evidence confirms Deel supports creating time-off requests via API/MCP (createTimeOffRequest) and ties into payroll/time data, but there is no evidence of defining custom PTO policies, accrual rules, or approval workflows that automatically feed into payroll calculations.
Evidence covers global payroll, contracts, MCP/API tooling, and sandbox docs, but nothing mentions 401(k), retirement plans, or benefits administration with automatic payroll-synced contributions.

Deel's marketing pages claim to 'run accurate, compliant payroll' and 'process payroll globally' across worker types, implying an end-to-end payroll capability, but no evidence details a specific review-hours/preview-totals/submit UI flow. Community feedback also warns of rigid, bug-prone workflows that break on exceptions.

The evidence pack contains only API/MCP/payroll documentation and negative community feedback; there is no mention of a self-serve onboarding flow, W-4/I-9 collection, or bank-detail intake for new hires anywhere in the provided items.

Evidence shows Deel supports contracts, time-off requests, and general payroll processing, but there is no mention of hourly time entries or overtime calculations flowing into payroll runs. No API/tool references to timesheets, hourly tracking, or overtime rules were found.

Evidence covers global payroll, contracts, API/MCP tooling, but nothing specifically addresses W-2/1099 tax form generation or distribution at year-end; no documentation or claims reference US tax filing forms.

Evidence pack mentions Gusto integrates with 'accounting' apps generally (gusto-docs-41) but provides no specifics on QuickBooks/Xero payroll journal entry syncing, mapping, or automation—no docs, community mentions, or feature details confirm this capability.

Gusto's Embedded Payroll API and docs cover company/employee onboarding building blocks (company details, employee tax info configuration, multi-location/department setup) and even ship an official MCP server letting AI agents like Claude/Cursor call the API directly, which supports agent-driven onboarding. However, the evidence pack lacks explicit documentation of a full employee+compensation creation endpoint sequence, so end-to-end 'onboard a new hire' via API is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

Gusto exposes an API and an official MCP server that lets AI agents interact directly with Embedded Payroll endpoints, and there is a contractor-payment preview endpoint (POST .../contractor_payment_groups/preview) plus GET unprocessed payrolls for review before submission — enabling agent-driven pre-run checks. However, there is no documented 'payroll preview' endpoint for regular employee payroll runs nor any built-in anomaly-detection/surfacing feature, so the anomaly-review capability would need to be built by the integrator rather than being a native product feature.

Gusto's Embedded Payroll API exposes payroll data (GET /payrolls), webhooks like payroll.paid, and general 'Generate payroll reports' functionality, plus a note that Gusto integrates with accounting apps — giving an agent plausible hooks to pull payroll data. However, there's no documented journal-entry/GL export schema or reconciliation-specific endpoint, and the MCP server (dev-assistant-mcp) is aimed at helping developers build against the API rather than at automating ledger reconciliation for an end user.

Gusto hosts a working llms.txt (HTTP 200, confirmed by probe) plus .md versions of docs pages, and also offers an official MCP server (Embedded Dev Assistant) enabling AI tools like Cursor, Windsurf, and Claude Desktop to query docs and interact with the API directly.

Gusto provides an MCP server that lets external AI coding tools (Cursor, Claude Desktop) interact with the Embedded Payroll API/docs for developers, but there is no evidence of in-product AI-generated insights or suggestions surfaced to end users from their own payroll/HR data.

Gusto provides webhooks, an API, and an MCP server for AI coding assistants to interact with docs/API, but there is no evidence of a mechanism for end users to build autonomous background automations (e.g., triggers/workflows/agents that run independently). The MCP server is a dev-assistant tool for coding, not an autonomous automation runtime.

The only AI-related evidence is the Embedded Dev Assistant MCP server, which lets external AI coding tools (Cursor, Claude Desktop) query Gusto's API docs for developers building integrations — it is not a built-in AI assistant inside the Gusto product that an end-user can delegate payroll/HR tasks to.

Gusto's Embedded Payroll API is fully REST-based (idempotency keys, webhooks, pagination, version fields) meaning core payroll operations can be automated headlessly/via CI, and there's an official MCP server for AI coding tools to interact with the API/docs. However, evidence is entirely for the separate 'Embedded Payroll' partner product (build-your-own payroll platform), not the mainstream Gusto SaaS app itself, and there's no explicit CLI/CI automation testing framework mentioned.

Gusto's documented MCP support (dev-assistant-mcp) runs in the opposite direction: it exposes an MCP server so external AI coding tools (Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Desktop) can query Gusto's API/docs. There is no evidence that Gusto itself can act as an MCP client, letting users plug in arbitrary MCP servers for Gusto to use their tools.

Gusto documents an official 'Embedded Dev Assistant' MCP server enabling AI tools like Cursor, Windsurf, and Claude Desktop to interact directly with the Embedded Payroll API and docs, confirmed by both docs claims and an independent probe hitting the live doc page.

Gusto offers an official 'Embedded Dev Assistant' MCP server letting AI tools like Cursor, Windsurf, and Claude Desktop interact with the Embedded Payroll API and docs, which is a genuine agentic/natural-language interface. However, this is scoped to developers building on the API, not end-users issuing natural-language commands to run payroll or HR tasks directly within the product.

Evidence shows Gusto offers an official MCP server (Embedded Dev Assistant) for AI tools like Cursor, Windsurf, and Claude Desktop to interact with its API/docs, but there is no mention anywhere in the docs of an official command-line interface (CLI) tool.

Gusto Embedded Payroll offers a comprehensive, well-documented public REST API covering payroll, contractors, time off, benefits, webhooks, pagination, idempotency, and versioning, plus an official MCP server enabling AI tools like Claude Desktop/Cursor to interact directly with the API and docs, confirmed via llms.txt and MCP-specific docs.

Evidence shows Gusto's API uses general authentication and an MCP server for AI tools to interact with the API, but there is no mention of scoped or least-privilege API credentials, granular permission tokens, or agent-specific credential issuance anywhere in the docs.

Gusto provides a well-documented REST API, webhooks, idempotency, and an official 'Embedded Dev Assistant' MCP server that lets AI tools like Cursor, Windsurf, and Claude Desktop interact directly with the API and docs, which supports AI-native development. However, there is no evidence of traditional official client SDKs (e.g., language-specific libraries) beyond the raw API and MCP integration.

Gusto's official docs describe a webhooks infrastructure with HTTP push events (e.g. payroll.paid), HMAC signature verification via verification_token, and recommends integrating for event-driven business logic — this directly matches subscribing to events via webhooks.

Evidence shows extensive markdown/LLM-readable docs and an MCP server for AI code editors, but there is no mention of an interactive API reference with runnable examples (e.g., a Swagger/Postman-style try-it-out console).
Evidence shows extensive API docs, an MCP server, and llms.txt machine-readable docs, but there is no mention of a downloadable OpenAPI spec or equivalent machine-readable API specification file.

Gusto's docs mention that 'Demo companies are automatically generated with company info, employees, and previous payrolls so you can begin testing right away,' implying a sandbox-like test environment separate from production. However, there is no explicit 'sandbox' terminology, no detail on isolation guarantees, and no community evidence confirming reliable sandbox testing for developers.

Evidence shows API fundamentals (versioning field on objects, idempotency, pagination) and even v1 URL paths, but there is no mention of API version lifecycle management or a documented deprecation policy for the API itself; nothing in the pack addresses how breaking changes or sunsetting of endpoints are communicated.

Gusto's platform docs explicitly promise automatic tax calculation, filing, multi-state compliance, and tax configuration (gusto-docs-44, gusto-docs-45, gusto-docs-37), which squarely covers this story. However, community evidence includes a specific, credible incident where Gusto mishandled W-2 tax filings, resulting in payroll being double-reported to the IRS with support unable to resolve it (gusto-comm-11), plus broader complaints about declining reliability of specialized tax support (gusto-comm-12, gusto-comm-13), directly contradicting the 'automatic and reliable' claim.

Gusto's API supports operations that inherently act on multiple items (running a regular or off-cycle payroll for an entire company, grouping contractor payments via contractor_payment_groups), and pagination exists for listing large sets of records, but there is no documented bulk/batch endpoint for arbitrary bulk create/update/delete across many resources at once, and no AI-native bulk-action tooling beyond the general MCP dev-assistant.

Gusto offers webhooks for reacting to events (e.g., payroll.paid) and an MCP server for AI code assistants to call the API, but there is no evidence of a user-facing rules engine or automation system where users can define 'if event X then action Y' triggers. Webhooks require the partner to build their own automation logic externally, not a native rule-definition capability.

Gusto's Embedded Payroll API supports regular payroll schedules and off-cycle payrolls, but there is no evidence of a general-purpose recurring job/workflow scheduling capability for AI-native automation—payroll schedules are fixed HR/payroll cadences, not user-configurable recurring workflows or agent-triggerable jobs.

Gusto is a payroll/HR API platform with no concept of 'automations' that a user builds, versions, or rolls back; the closest feature is a record 'version' field used for optimistic concurrency control on API updates (409 conflict), not automation versioning/review/rollback. No evidence of any automation-building, workflow versioning, or rollback capability exists in the evidence pack.

Docs describe off-cycle payrolls for handling 'corrections' and distinguish 'unprocessed' vs processed payroll status, implying some ability to adjust before payment, but there is no explicit documented capability to cancel/void a submitted payroll run before employees are paid.

The evidence pack covers Gusto's Embedded Payroll API (payroll processing, webhooks, contractor payments, time off) but contains no mention of proactive compliance alerting for new hires, new locations, or law changes. No feature described notifies founders of emerging compliance obligations.

Gusto Embedded Payroll is a comprehensive, well-documented partner API/platform explicitly designed for embedding payroll, HR, benefits, and contractor payments into third-party products, with pre-built UI flows, webhooks, idempotency, and multi-state/tax handling. Extensive first-party docs and a verified live documentation site confirm this is a mature, purpose-built offering, though evidence is vendor-sourced with no independent developer reviews.

Gusto's docs explicitly state support for next-day, 2-day, and standard 4-day payroll processing via direct deposit, replacing manual checks, and this is corroborated by a community reviewer who used Gusto's 2-day payroll feature (though noting a $60k cap needing support exceptions).

Docs confirm companies can have multiple work locations and 'prefer different pay schedules,' and platform overview mentions multi-location management, implying support for varied schedules across teams. However, no explicit mention of specific frequency options (weekly, biweekly, semimonthly, monthly) or configuration details, so full capability isn't clearly evidenced.

No documentation evidence describes EOR or owned-entity global payroll offerings; all API/docs content is scoped to US payroll, contractors, and taxes. Community evidence explicitly states 'Gusto doesn't support outside of US folks' and that multi-country employee benefits could not be customized, contradicting any international employment capability.

Docs confirm Gusto offers health insurance through a SimplyInsured partnership and lists benefits/deductions as part of its platform (gusto-docs-39, gusto-docs-45), but there's no explicit documentation of deduction-to-payroll sync mechanics, and community reports describe real-world friction — inability to customize plans across states, platform lock-in for benefit features like HSA, and a costly failure to terminate a health plan correctly.

Gusto's documented contractor payment methods are limited to direct deposit, check, and historical payment with no mention of local-currency international payouts or compliant international contracts. Community evidence explicitly states 'Gusto doesn't support outside of US folks,' directly contradicting the international contractor use case.

Gusto's docs explicitly claim multi-location/multi-state support, automatic tax calculation and filing, and handling of multi-state tax requirements as core platform features (docs-31, docs-44, docs-45). However, this evidence is primarily vendor documentation rather than hands-on validation, and community feedback raises real concerns about tax/compliance execution issues (W-2 corrections, double-reported payroll to IRS, healthcare/benefits mismanagement across states) that undercut confidence in flawless multi-state compliance.

Gusto's docs explicitly define off-cycle payrolls for bonuses, corrections, or terminations outside the regular schedule, with a dedicated guide for creating them and specific handling like bonus tax withholding rules, indicating clear API/product support.
The evidence pack covers Gusto Embedded Payroll's payroll, contractor, time-off, and benefits APIs, but contains no mention of offer letters, e-signature workflows, or document storage per employee.

Gusto's Embedded Payroll docs show a comprehensive REST API covering payroll runs, off-cycle payrolls, contractor payments, time-off requests, tax configuration, webhooks, idempotency, and pagination — and even ties in AI tooling directly via an official MCP server for Cursor/Windsurf/Claude Desktop, strongly supporting API-native workflows. However, several capabilities (e.g., 401(k) Guideline enrollment, some time-off approval UX, other benefit partner integrations) are explicitly delivered via Gusto's 'pre-built UI Flows' rather than pure API calls, and docs frame API vs. Flows as alternative approaches rather than guaranteeing full parity, so full 1:1 API/UI equivalence isn't confirmed.

Gusto is an embedded payroll/HR platform aimed at partner companies, not end-users; the evidence shows no data export/portability feature for an individual user to export their own data in open formats and leave. Docs focus on API access for building integrations, not self-service full data export for account closure/migration.

Gusto is a closed-source proprietary payroll/HR SaaS platform; there is no evidence of any open-licensed source code being available for inspection. All evidence relates to API docs, community reviews, and MCP tooling, none of which indicates source code openness.

Gusto is a SaaS payroll/HR platform with no self-hosting option; the evidence pack shows only embedded APIs, webhooks, and hosted flows, none of which involve deploying the core product on user infrastructure.

Docs clearly show Gusto supports both regular/off-cycle employee payroll (with tax withholding, multi-state, direct deposit) and separate contractor payment APIs with direct deposit/check/historical methods, all within one platform (docs-9,18,26,27,44). However, the evidence pack does not show specific webhook events for 'employee onboarded' or 'payment failed', so full breadth of lifecycle events claimed in the story is unconfirmed.

Docs list 'Generate payroll reports' as a platform capability, implying some reporting exists, but there is no detail on payroll register or gross-to-net report generation, formats, or export/analysis tooling beyond that single bullet point.

No evidence in the pack addresses data residency, regional storage options, or data location controls for Gusto; Gusto also appears US-focused (per community note that it 'doesn't support outside of US folks'), but nothing confirms or denies configurable data residency.

No evidence in the pack addresses AI training data usage, opt-out controls, or any privacy policy regarding AI model training on customer data. Gusto's documentation focuses entirely on payroll/HR API functionality with no mention of AI training data governance.

The evidence pack contains no documentation or discussion of data retention policies, data deletion controls, or privacy/data governance settings for AI-native users; Gusto's docs focus on payroll, contractors, and API mechanics with no mention of retention/deletion capabilities.
No evidence in the pack addresses telemetry/usage-tracking opt-out controls for Gusto; documentation focuses on payroll API functionality with no privacy/telemetry settings mentioned.

Gusto documents a 401(k) offering through its partnership with Guideline, with pre-built flows letting admins access Guideline via Gusto Embedded, alongside other embedded benefits like health insurance and workers comp — implying payroll data integration but not explicitly confirming automatic per-payroll contribution syncing.

No evidence of any Justworks API for payroll data, let alone a payroll preview/run endpoint; probes show no OpenAPI/API discovery surface exists, and all docs describe manual UI workflows only.
